                      NRG ENERGY, INC.’S COMMENTS ON PROPOSED RULE
        NRG Energy, Inc. (NRG) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the rule proposed by the
Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT or Commission) 1 regarding large load interconnection
standards to implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) 2 § 37.0561 adopted by the Texas
Legislature through Senate Bill 6 (SB6) in the 89th Legislative Session 3 (hereafter, Proposed Rule).
NRG is the parent company of established retail electric providers (REPs) and power generation
companies (PGCs) in the competitive electricity markets in Texas.
                                                   INTRODUCTION

        NRG appreciates the opportunity to provide input on the Proposed Rule regarding large load
interconnection standards introduced through SB6 and commends the Commission and Staff for
incorporating feedback in the Proposed Rule from earlier rounds of comment in this proceeding. The
large load interconnection standards are critical to get “right,” as the Electric Reliability Council of
Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) region faces unprecedented load growth in the next five years, which will bring
both challenges for the grid and significant opportunities for business development in the state. In
anticipation of this growth, the Legislature set complimentary goals for the Commission to balance in
implementing the large load interconnection standards required by PURA § 37.0561—i.e., to both
“support business development in this state while [also] minimizing the potential for stranded
infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.” 4

        The Proposed Rule has incorporated some helpful recommendations from prior comments, such
as reducing the financial commitment per megawatt (MW) from $100,000 to $50,000 and adding
options to lease or purchase property as proof of site control at the intermediate agreement phase. NRG
proposes additional changes below, which it views as needed to fully achieve the statutory aims:

 PROJECT NO. 58481 – LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS
•   Refund availability: The refund provisions should be modified as follows:
    o      Early withdrawal: A large load customer that withdraws before signing an
           interconnection agreement should receive 80% of its financial security back, instead of
           forfeiting 80% of it, to refrain from punishing large loads that prudently withdraw their
           projects (e.g., after learning the results of the interconnection study process).
    o      Post-energization: A large load customer that energizes should be refunded 50% of its
           $50,000 per MW interconnection fee, as well as 50% of any posted financial security
           for system upgrades and long-lead time equipment, upon energization (rather than
           forfeiting 100% of the interconnection fee and receiving only 20% of other financial
           security back at that time), to incentivize large loads that sign an interconnection
           agreement to complete construction and energize.
•   Support for “bring-your-own-generation”: BYOG arrangements will help address future
    affordability and reliability issues and thus should be encouraged to the greatest extent possible.
    Support for BYOG in this Proposed Rule can be accomplished by calculating the per MW
    financial security requirement based on the anticipated net load to the site during summer peak,
    and sites that will be net exporters should not owe the $50,000 per MW financial security or
    interconnection fee.
•   Credit for self-supplied equipment: Large load customers should get credit, against the financial
    security requirement for long-lead time equipment or services, for any equipment that they
    procure themselves and that the interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP) or
    distribution service provider (DSP), as applicable, accepts for use.
•   Drawing down security for long-lead time equipment to fund CIAC: Similarly, the security for
    long-lead time equipment or services, to the extent related to direct interconnection costs, should
    be drawn down to help fund the contribution in aid of construction (CIAC), before imposing a
    direct payment obligation on the large load.
•   Broadening acceptable forms of security: The acceptable forms of security should include
    corporate guaranty agreements by a corporate sponsor, as well as surety bonds.
•   Modification to timelines:
    o      ERCOT and the interconnecting utility should coordinate regarding initiation of the
           interconnection study within 30 days (rather than 60 days) of executing the intermediate
           agreement to give the large load a better chance to get into the next batch (once that
           process is implemented); and

         o        Large load customers should have 60 days (rather than 30 days) to execute an
                  interconnection agreement following completion of the required study since substantial
                  non-refundable commitments are triggered at that point.
•        Softening reallocation requirements for reasonable project delays: A large load customer’s
         capacity should not be reallocated to another customer if the customer fails to satisfy a milestone
         in its phased energization so long as the customer is making reasonable efforts at development,
         and the large load customer should be able to amend its ramp schedule up until it provides the

                                      COMMENTS ON PROPOSED RULE

    1. Subsection (d) – Intermediate Agreement

         a. Subsection (d)(7) – Power supply

         NRG conceptually supports the Proposed Rule’s requirement for large load customers to
disclose power procurement plans, including whether they will have on-site generation, and to make
this a separate disclosure from the one regarding backup generation. By statutory (and Proposed Rule)
definition, backup generation will run only on a limited basis, as it cannot be configured to operate in
parallel with or export energy to the ERCOT system. 6 The substantial influx of large load customers to
Texas, as described further below, creates imminent affordability and reliability concerns for average
Texans. Thus, it is prudent for the Commission to require large load customers to disclose how they
intend to procure power and, specifically, whether they intend to co-locate with on-site generation that
is sufficient to serve their peak demand and even export to the ERCOT grid (e.g., to be oversized).
NRG proposes some modifications to the language, below, to ensure that the required disclosure will
inform the interconnecting utility and ERCOT as to whether the large load customer plans to bring its
own on-site generation to run in parallel with the grid (as compared to backup generation only) and
whether that generation will be sufficient to meet (or even exceed) the large load customer’s peak
demand:



       5
         In addition to the changes discussed further in the comments above, NRG has also proposed non-substantive
grammatical and clean-up edits to subsection (c), definitions, in Attachment A to these comments.
         6
            See PURA § 37.0561(e) (“For the purposes of this subsection, ‘on-site backup generating facilities’ means
generation that is not capable of exporting energy to the ERCOT transmission grid and that, in the aggregate, can serve at
least 50 percent of on-site demand.”); Proposed Rule at Subsection (c)(1) (“Backup generating facilities – Generation
facilities or energy storage facilities that are not capable of operating, or are not configured to operate, in parallel with the
ERCOT system and cannot export energy to the ERCOT system.”) (emphasis in original).

        (7)     Power supply. A large load customer must disclose how it plans to procure power and
                whether the large load customer has will have on-site, co-located generation that will
                provide power sufficient exclusively to serve the peak demand of the large load
                customer. This disclosure shall provide the anticipated summer net dependable
                capability for any on-site, co-located generation.

        b. Subsection (d)(10) – Financial security on a dollar per MW basis

        As an initial matter, NRG supports the proposed $50,000 per MW value in the Proposed Rule,
but recommends changes to the introductory paragraph of this section to incentivize BYOG
arrangements. The dollar per MW financial security is one of the most critical parts of the Proposed
Rule that, if set at the right value, should go a long way toward bringing discipline to the large load
queue, which is currently at an unprecedented and unachievable level. In the March 2026 update on the
large load queue to the Technical Advisory Committee, ERCOT reports over 410 gigawatts (GW) in
the queue for 2030: 7




         7
             ERCOT       Large    Load    Integration Status   Update   (Mar.    26,   2026),   available       at:
https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/03/27/March-TAC-Report-Updated_03262026.pptx.
NRG COMMENTS ON PROPOSED RULE                                                                               4
 PROJECT NO. 58481 – LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS
        For context, 410 GW is more than quadruple the current record peak demand of 85.5 GW from
August 10, 2023 8 and would dwarf the annual load growth typically seen in ERCOT. 9 Even excluding
the capacity for which no studies have been submitted for 2030 (~293 GW), the remaining amount of
large load in the queue (~117 GW) still exceeds the existing peak demand by over 30 GW. It is highly
unlikely, if not impossible, that the ERCOT system could physically interconnect and accommodate
such a large amount of electricity demand on that timeline. It is also equally unlikely that the supply
chain for data center equipment could support that amount of development in 5 years or less. Setting
an appropriately high financial security figure (like the $50,000 per MW value in the Proposed Rule),
coupled with appropriate refund policies (as proposed later below), should help bring discipline to the
large load queue, remove the “noise,” and enable utilities and ERCOT to process requests by the
projects that are likely to energize.

        While NRG believes the proposed $50,000 per MW value is appropriate the financial security
amount, the Proposed Rule should be revised to promote business structures that would help ERCOT
integrate the substantial amount of large loads planning to energize in the next 5 years and would help
address both the growing affordability and reliability issues facing average Texans. Specifically, for
large load customers that will bring new, dispatchable generation to co-locate on their site and provide
sufficient, or even excess, power to serve their expected peak demand, the financial security amount
should be set to recognize that these large loads will not import from (and may even export to) the
ERCOT grid during the summer peak. Today, when ERCOT includes private use networks in its Report
on the Capacity, Demand and Reserves in the ERCOT Region (CDR), ERCOT measures the
contribution associated with private use networks based on their “average available power during the
seasonal peak days over the past three years” and “adjusted for any reported changes in capacity at the
start of the forecast season.” 10 A similar methodology could be used to calculate the “requested peak
demand” for purposes of determining the required financial security requirement under subsection
(d)(10) of the Proposed Rule (as well as the interconnection fee amount under proposed subsection
(f)(7)), except that the value could be based on the estimated net contribution (or need) during summer
peak.

        For example, if a 500 MW planned large load will develop a natural gas generation facility with
an estimated summer net dependable capability of 600 MW, then the site would be expected to be a net
exporter (i.e., +100 MW) to the ERCOT grid during summer peak, and the large load customer would
not owe financial security under this provision or subsection (f)(7); similarly, if the generation facility
in that example would equal the peak demand (i.e., at 500 MW), then no financial security would be
owed under these sections. This makes sense because the funding required from the large load customer
to bring new generation greatly exceeds the $50,000/MW financial security amount so concerns about
whether the large load can meet financial commitments are easily satisfied with BYOG arrangements.
If the on-site generation would be undersized compared to the large load, then financial security would
be owed for the expected net import to the grid during summer peak. In any event, such large load
customers still would be subject to the other financial commitment requirements set out in the Proposed
Rule, i.e., security for both long-lead time equipment/services and system upgrades and payment of
CIAC.

        NRG’s proposed language is below:

        (10)   Financial security on a dollar per MW basis. Financial security under this subsection
               is due at the time that the intermediate agreement is executed. A large load customer
               must post financial security with the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP in
               the amount of $50,000 per MW of the requested peak demand for new interconnection
               requests or of the incremental increase in the peak demand for expanded interconnection
               requests. For a large load that will co-locate with new dispatchable generation, the peak
               demand for financial security purposes will be calculated based on the estimated net
               export to or import from the ERCOT grid during the summer peak, as calculated
               consistent with the methodology used by ERCOT in the annual report on capacity,
               demand and reserves for private use networks. A large load co-located with new
               dispatchable generation that will not consume power from the grid or will be a net
               exporter of energy during the summer peak will owe no financial security under this
               section (d)(10).

        c. Subsection (d)(10)(C) – (E) – Acceptable forms of financial security

        NRG recommends proposed subsection (d)(10)(C) and (D) be revised to expressly allow for a
designated sponsor to provide the parental guaranty, as an alternative to the large load customer. The
identity of the large load customer may change during the project, especially in co-location
arrangements where a generation developer may initially make the request on behalf of a large load
that will co-locate at the site while the agreement with the co-located load is still in negotiations. The
Proposed Rule already recognizes the ability for a “corporate” guaranty, but does not expressly state
that the guaranty may be provided by a corporate sponsor that is not affiliated with the large load

requirements for long-lead time equipment that the large load customer procures itself, subject to the
acceptance of that equipment by the interconnecting DSP or TSP. NRG understands that interconnecting

      2. Subsection (e) – Interconnection Study

         NRG recommends two changes to proposed subsection (e). First, the deadline for the
interconnecting DSP or TSP to “coordinate with ERCOT to initiate an interconnection study” should
be shortened from 60 days to 30 days. With the new batch process under development at ERCOT, this
initial coordination should occur as expediently as possible, to ensure that a large load customer has the
opportunity to qualify for the soonest available batch process window, rather than potentially missing
that window and having to wait a year or more for the next window. Second, proposed subsection (e)(4)
should only require a “new interconnection request” following a request for additional capacity if
ERCOT and the interconnecting DSP or TSP deem that necessary. In other words, the proposed rule
should allow ERCOT and the interconnecting DSP or TSP to exercise discretion in determining whether
a particular request for additional capacity requires any additional study (and thus necessitates a new
interconnection request) rather than requiring a new request as a matter of course:

(e)      Interconnection study. Not later than 6030 days after an intermediate agreement is executed
         under subsection (d) of this section, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must
         coordinate with ERCOT to initiate an interconnection study.

      3. Subsection (f) – Interconnection Agreement

         Proposed subsection (f) (introductory paragraph) should allow 60 days (rather than only 30
days) for the large load customer to evaluate the results of the interconnection study, secure necessary
financing, and execute the interconnection agreement. The execution of the interconnection agreement
is a critical step in the interconnection process—particularly if the Commission agrees with NRG’s
proposal to modify the refund structure to allow a more substantial refund if the load withdraws before
executing the interconnection agreement, but to eliminate any refund if the load withdraws after
executing that agreement. The Proposed Rule should allow sufficient time for the large load customer
to determine whether to enter the substantial, financially binding commitment that the execution of the
interconnection agreement would trigger. Sixty days (or approximately 2 months) would be a more
reasonable timeframe for this purpose than 30 days.

requires corresponding changes to subsection (f)(7), as proposed below. Conceptually, NRG agrees
with the apparent intent of the Proposed Rule to ensure that TSPs use any non-refundable financial

       c. Subsection (f)(9) – Contribution in aid of construction (CIAC)

       Proposed subsection (f)(9) should allow for the use of financial security for long-lead time
equipment to be drawn down for the payment of CIAC, to the extent that the long-lead time equipment
relates to direct interconnection costs. The current Proposed Rule appears to assume that the financial
security for long-lead time equipment will be unrelated to the CIAC requirement and thus does not
attempt to tie these two concepts together. However, it is possible that the CIAC will include some or
all of the same long-lead time equipment for which the large load customer posted security under
subsection (d)(11) at the intermediate phase and under subsection (f)(8) at the interconnection
agreement phase. Thus, the rule should recognize this possibility and allow for the financial security
for long-lead time equipment to be drawn down for CIAC if the equipment for which the security was
posted relates to direct interconnection costs. Further, the rule should address a circumstance where the
financial security posted under subsection (f)(8) exceeds the actual cost of CIAC and relates to direct
interconnection costs (e.g., if the CIAC was over-securitized based on the financial security posted
under subsection (f)(8) or potentially posted during the intermediate phase under subsection (d)(11),
which must be applied to any security owed under subsection (f)(8)). In that event, the rule should

       NRG supports the concept of using the financial commitment required under this rule to offset
rate impacts for smaller customers, particularly the residential class, and thus supports making the
interconnection fee partially non-refundable. However, the Proposed Rule also should incentivize large
load customers to energize and achieve their ramp. As the Proposed Rule is currently drafted, a large
load customer that withdraws after posting the interconnection fee (i.e., at the interconnection
agreement phase) is financially in the same position as a large load customer that follows through with
its request and energizes as planned—in that, the fee would be non-refundable in both instances. Thus,
the current Proposed Rule creates no incentive for large loads to energize, which would be a substantial
waste of time for ERCOT, TSPs, and DSPs and would negatively impact other large loads that are
serious about energizing and awaiting their turn in the upcoming batch process.

requirements to balance the goals of supporting business development in the state and avoiding stranded
costs and maintaining reliability. 20 Making the interconnection fee entirely non-refundable may help
avoid stranded costs (and potentially help with reliability to the extent it brings discipline to the queue
and thus makes it more manageable for ERCOT to reliably interconnect). But it likely does not further
the goal of supporting business development, especially given the relatively high amount of the fee
($50,000/MW) coupled with the fact that it is only one piece of several financial commitment

                             NRG ENERGY, INC.’S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

•   NRG commends the Commission and Staff for incorporating feedback in the Proposed Rule from earlier
    rounds of comment in this proceeding such as reducing the financial commitment per MW from $100,000
    to $50,000 and adding options to lease or purchase property as proof of site control at the intermediate
    agreement phase.
•   The large load interconnection standards are critical to get “right,” as the ERCOT region faces unprecedented
    load growth in the next five years, which will bring both challenges for the grid and significant opportunities
    for business development in the state. In anticipation of this growth, the Legislature set complimentary goals
    for the Commission to balance in implementing the large load interconnection standards required by PURA
    § 37.0561—i.e., to both “support business development in this state while [also] minimizing the potential
    for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.” To fully achieve the statutory aims,
    NRG supports additional changes to the Proposed Rule, as detailed below.
•   Refund availability: The refund provisions should be modified as follows:
    o Early withdrawal: A large load customer that withdraws before signing an interconnection agreement
         should receive 80% of its financial security back, instead of forfeiting 80% of it, to refrain from
         punishing large loads that prudently withdraw their projects (e.g., after learning the results of the
         interconnection study process).
    o Post-energization: A large load customer that energizes should be refunded 50% of its $50,000 per MW
         interconnection fee, as well as 50% of any posted financial security for system upgrades and long-lead
         time equipment, upon energization (rather than forfeiting 100% of the interconnection fee and receiving
         only 20% of other financial security back at that time), to incentivize large loads that sign an
         interconnection agreement to complete construction and energize.
•   Use of funds retained by the utility: NRG supports Staff’s suggestion in Project No. 59142 to replace “rate
    base” with “annual revenue requirement” for purposes of what interconnecting utilities must do with retained
    funds, to ensure that non-large load customers (particularly residential customers) are protected.
•   Support for “bring-your-own-generation”: BYOG arrangements will help address future affordability and
    reliability issues and thus should be encouraged to the greatest extent possible. Support for BYOG in this
    Proposed Rule can be accomplished by calculating the per MW financial security requirement based on the
    anticipated net load to the site during summer peak, and sites that will be net exporters (or net zero) should
    not owe the $50,000 per MW financial security or interconnection fee.
•   Credit for self-supplied equipment: Large load customers should get credit, against the financial security
    requirement for long-lead time equipment or services, for any equipment that they procure themselves and
    that the interconnecting TSP or DSP, as applicable, accepts for use.
•   Drawing down security for long-lead time equipment to fund CIAC: Similarly, the security for long-lead
    time equipment or services, to the extent related to direct interconnection costs, should be drawn down to
    help fund the CIAC, before imposing a direct payment obligation on the large load.
•   Broadening acceptable forms of security: The acceptable forms of security should include corporate guaranty
    agreements by a corporate sponsor, as well as surety bonds.
•   Modification to timelines:
    o ERCOT and the interconnecting utility should coordinate regarding initiation of the interconnection
         study within 30 days (rather than 60 days) of executing the intermediate agreement to give the large load
         a better chance to get into the next batch (once that process is implemented); and
    o Large load customers should have 60 days (rather than 30 days) to execute an interconnection agreement
         following completion of the required study since substantial non-refundable commitments are triggered
         at that point.
•   Softening reallocation requirements for reasonable project delays: A large load customer’s capacity should
    not be reallocated to another customer if the customer fails to satisfy a milestone in its phased energization
    so long as the customer is making reasonable efforts at development, and the large load customer should be
    able to amend its ramp schedule up until it provides the notice to proceed to the interconnecting utility.

    4. Subsection (g) - Withdrawal of Request

         NRG supports changes to the Proposed Rule to impose increasing financial commitment
obligations at different stages of the process, in order to help discipline the existing queue, while also
avoiding punitive requirements that may deter business development in Texas, contrary to the
framework set out in SB6.19 At the intermediate agreement phase in the Proposed Rule, the large load
customer will not yet have been studied (e.g., will not have gone through the upcoming batch process
yet) and will not know whether the interconnecting TSP or DSP or the ERCOT system can
accommodate its requested capacity. The rational economic decision at the conclusion of the study may
be for the large load customer to withdraw its request. However, as proposed, the rule would require
the large load customer to forfeit 80% of its financial security-including $50,000 per MW plus any
security posted for long-lead time equipment-for making an economically rational decision to
withdraw based on the results of the interconnection study process. NRG recommends that the
percentages be flipped, and the large load customer that withdraws before executing an interconnection
agreement should receive 80% of its financial security back and forfeit only 20% of it. Some financial
stake should be required to get into the interconnection study (e.g., the upcoming batch process) in the
first place, so it is appropriate for some of the financial security to be non-refundable at the intermediate
agreement phase. But, NRG posits that a 20% stake at this stage is more appropriate than an 80% stake.

         On the other hand, if a large load customer decides to execute an interconnection agreement
(i.e., which would be after the interconnection study process is complete), then the large load customer
should be financially committed from that point forward, which would create an incentive to energize
as planned. In other words, the customer should receive no refund if they execute the interconnection
agreement and then withdraw their request rather than energizing.

applicable" to acknowledge the possibility that a large load customer may have paid interconnection
fees (and not just posted financial security for such fees) before executing the interconnection
agreement and before deciding to withdraw its request. So long as the large load customer has not
executed the interconnection agreement, the customer should still be able to withdraw and receive an

      5. Subsection (h) - Non-utilized Capacity

         Proposed subsection (h) requires that "non-utilized" capacity be reallocated to a new large load
customer-i.e., with "non-utilized" effectively defined as the customer missing an energization
milestone by at least 6 months (plus a 30-day notice period). As a general matter, NRG agrees
conceptually with this framework to encourage large load customers to meet their milestones and
energize on schedule, but also notes that delays can occur despite a customer's diligent best efforts to
stay on schedule. Further, the schedule itself is typically subject to change until the customer provides
the interconnecting TSP or DSP with notice-to-proceed with construction of interconnection facilities.
In light of these realities, NRG recommends a few changes to this subsection. First, the large load
customer should be able to amend the milestone schedule that it will be held to following energization,
up until providing the notice to proceed. Second, the large load customer's capacity should not be
deemed "non-utilized" and reallocated to another customer if it can demonstrate it is making reasonable
efforts to continue development at the site. Third, NRG recommends adding "interconnection fees" to
the list of financial commitments that will be refunded to the customer if its capacity is reallocated,
consistent with NRG's recommendations below (under subsection (i)) to make that fee partially
refundable.

   6. Subsection (i) - Terms for Refund

       NRG supports the concept of using the financial commitment required under this rule to offset
rate impacts for smaller customers, particularly the residential class, and thus supports making the
interconnection fee partially non-refundable. However, the Proposed Rule also should incentivize large
load customers to energize and achieve their ramp. As the Proposed Rule is currently drafted, a large
load customer that withdraws after posting the interconnection fee (i.e., at the interconnection
agreement phase) is financially in the same position as a large load customer that follows through with
its request and energizes as planned-in that, the fee would be non-refundable in both instances. Thus,
the current Proposed Rule creates no incentive for large loads to energize, which would be a substantial
waste of time for ERCOT, TSPs, and DSPs and would negatively impact other large loads that are
serious about energizing and awaiting their turn in the upcoming batch process.

       Further, as noted above, one of the overarching requirements of SB6 is for the interconnection
requirements to balance the goals of supporting business development in the state and avoiding stranded
costs and maintaining reliability.20 Making the interconnection fee entirely non-refundable may help
avoid stranded costs (and potentially help with reliability to the extent it brings discipline to the queue
and thus makes it more manageable for ERCOT to reliably interconnect). But it likely does not further
the goal of supporting business development, especially given the relatively high amount of the fee
($50,000/MW) coupled with the fact that it is only one piece of several financial commitment

(a)   Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility,

                             NRG ENERGY. INC.'S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

•   NRG commends the Commission and Staff for incorporating feedback in the Proposed Rule from earlier
    rounds of comment in this proceeding such as reducing the financial commitment per MW from $100,000
    to $50,000 and adding options to lease or purchase property as proof of site control at the intermediate
    agreement phase.
•   The large load interconnection standards are critical to get "right," as the ERCOT region faces unprecedented
    load growth in the next five years, which will bring both challenges for the grid and significant opportunities
    for business development in the state. In anticipation ofthis growth, the Legislature set complimentary goals
    for the Commission to balance in implementing the large load interconnection standards required by PURA
    § 37.0561-i.e., to both "support business development in this state while [alsol minimizing the potential
    for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability." To fully achieve the statutory aims,
    NRG supports additional changes to the Proposed Rule, as detailed below.
•   Refund availabilitv: The refund provisions should be modified as follows:
    o   Earlv withdrawal: A large load customer that withdraws before signing an interconnection agreement
        should receive 80% of its financial security back, instead of forfeiting 80% of it, to refrain from
        punishing large loads that prudently withdraw their projects (e.g., after learning the results of the
        interconnection study process).
    o   Post-energization: A large load customer that energizes should be refunded 50% of its $50,000 per MW
        interconnection fee, as well as 50% of any posted financial security for system upgrades and long-lead
        time equipment, upon energization (rather than forfeiting 100% ofthe interconnection fee and receiving
        only 20% of other financial security back at that time), to incentivize large loads that sign an
        interconnection agreement to complete construction and energize.
•   Use of funds retained bv the utilitv: NRG supports Staff's suggestion in Project No. 59142 to replace "rate
    base" with "annual revenue requirement" for purposes ofwhat interconnecting utilities must do with retained
    funds, to ensure that non-large load customers (particularly residential customers) are protected.
•   Support for "bring-your-own-generation": BYOG arrangements will help address future affordability and
    reliability issues and thus should be encouraged to the greatest extent possible. Support for BYOG in this
    Proposed Rule can be accomplished by calculating the per MW financial security requirement based on the
    anticipated net load to the site during summer peak, and sites that will be net exporters (or net zero) should
    not owe the $50,000 per MW financial security or interconnection fee.
•   Credit for self-supplied equipment: Large load customers should get credit, against the financial security
    requirement for long-lead time equipment or services, for any equipment that they procure themselves and
    that the interconnecting TSP or DSP, as applicable, accepts for use.
•   Drawing down securitv for long-lead time equipment to fund CMC: Similarly, the security for long-lead
    time equipment or services, to the extent related to direct interconnection costs, should be drawn down to
    help fund the CMC, before imposing a direct payment obligation on the large load.
•   Broadening acceptable forms of securitv: The acceptable forms ofsecurity should include corporate guaranty
    agreements by a corporate sponsor, as well as surety bonds.
•   Modification to timelines:
    o   ERCOT and the interconnecting utility should coordinate regarding initiation of the interconnection
        study within 30 days (rather than 60 days) ofexecuting the intermediate agreement to give the large load
        a better chance to get into the next batch (once that process is implemented); and
    o   Large load customers should have 60 days (rather than 30 days) to execute an interconnection agreement
        following completion ofthe required study since substantial non-refundable commitments are triggered
        at that point.
•   Softening reallocation requirements for reasonable project delays: A large load customer's capacity should
    not be reallocated to another customer ifthe customer fails to satisfy a milestone in its phased energization
    so long as the customer is making reasonable efforts at development, and the large load customer should be
    able to amend its ramp schedule up until it provides the notice to proceed to the interconnecting utility.
